name: Profit as the firm's one responsibility
idea: The work holds that in a free society business has one social responsibility: to use its resources to raise profits within the rules of the game. The executive answers to the owners for running the business as they wish, which generally means earning as much as possible within law and ethical custom. Spending their money on social aims they would not choose amounts in effect to imposing a tax.
suggests: Look at what a company spends on social or environmental aims, and ask whether each outlay serves its own long-run interest or spends owners', customers' or employees' money on aims they did not choose.
limits: The work treats a sole proprietor somewhat differently: one who gives up returns for social aims spends his own money, not someone else's. It also grants that a major employer in a small community may serve its own long-run interest by funding amenities there.
competing_idea: Another view, which the work sets out, holds that pressing problems cannot wait for slow political processes, so that businessmen taking on social responsibility solve them more quickly and surely. The work rejects this on grounds of principle.
questions: Which of the company's social or environmental outlays would it make anyway, because they serve its own long-run interest?
Whose money pays for an outlay that does not: the owners', the customers' through prices, or the employees' through wages?
Who decided on these outlays, and through what process were owners or the public consulted?

originals.reference: Milton Friedman, "A Friedman doctrine-- The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits", The New York Times, 13 September 1970, Section SM, p. 17 (the newspaper's digitized archive text)
